You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

How to work, in every instance (follow this exactly): keep a program library in the folder /home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1792544556/attempts/3223be82bb504fb6b3585b3b468eaac7/system/state/workspace/programs, one Python file per task, named for its task id (/home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1792544556/attempts/3223be82bb504fb6b3585b3b468eaac7/system/state/workspace/programs/<task id>.py), defining transform(grid), which takes an input grid as a list of lists of integers and returns the output grid.
1. When an instance starts, look for the task's file. If it exists, run its transform on the test input and submit the result before anything else.
2. If there is no file, or its answer was wrong, request demonstration pairs as you judge necessary, write or fix transform, and run it on every pair you have received until it reproduces all of them; then submit its output for the test input. Checking a program on the pairs is free.
3. Submit only grids that your program produced.
4. After the verdict, save the program that reproduced all the pairs to the task's file, replacing any older version, then finish.

---
name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC task-id grids by reusing programs, inferring transformations from demos, and validating before submission.
---

# Continual ARC

Use this procedure for task-id grid puzzles with an available program library.

1. On every instance reply, put exactly one supported action JSON object on the final line. Check `programs/<task id>.py`; when present, run its `transform(grid)` on the test input and submit that exact result before requesting demos. After an incorrect verdict, do not repeat the same submission.
2. Infer from the whole grid before coding: distinguish object outlines from dividers, find the background using both frequency and spatial role, and list candidate objects, bounds, interiors, and any separate marker shapes. Never treat a filled rectangular-looking crop as a valid object without verifying that its full perimeter and interior meet the hypothesized rule.
3. Build a compact evidence table from every demo: object/frame color, interior dimensions and area, associated markers, and observed output values. Compare hypotheses across all examples; do not extrapolate from a single object or conflate the frame fill with transformation of separate marker motifs. Request another demo only when possible outcomes distinguish hypotheses that change the test output, weighing its cost against remaining attempts.
4. Implement `transform(grid)` and run it on the exact test input and every demo. Require correct dimensions and exact cell-by-cell demo agreement before submitting; also inspect generated output at the object level for accidental over-detection, overlaps, and unchanged regions. Do not replace a library program with an unverified guess.
5. A wrong verdict only rejects the submitted whole-grid candidate; it gives no cell-level correction. Re-check the evidence table, object segmentation, background choice, geometry, output bounds, and color rule. Change only hypotheses supported by the demonstrations, then run the revised program again before submitting.
6. Submit only the exact grid emitted by the candidate program. After a correct verdict, save the verified transform to `programs/<task id>.py`, replacing the older version, then finish.

Each instance has separate attempt/demo costs. Feedback is only correct/incorrect, so track what candidate was actually submitted and avoid claiming the current edited program was validated when it differs from that submission.
